title: A Hidden Limit of Space and Time Could Lead to Ultrafast Electronics
summary: Quantum physics has a rule: you cannot know everything about a particle at once. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says a particle's position and momentum cannot both be measured exactly. But position and time are different. Now scientists have shown another limit: an electron's location and its behaviour over time cannot both be pinned down exactly. This new 'space-time limit' could matter for quantum technology and ultrafast electronics. The discovery comes from a team in Regensburg, Germany, working with colleagues in Hamburg. To watch electrons move, the team built a new laser system that works like a high-speed camera. Timed laser pulses drive electrons from a sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The movements happen over attoseconds: one attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. At these distances, electrons move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms. Instead of moving like tiny balls, the electrons behave as quantum waves, letting them pass through an energy barrier they should not be able to cross. This is quantum tunnelling, a bit like passing through a solid wall without breaking it.
why_it_matters: If you use a phone or a computer, this science could one day help make them much, much faster.

background_read: Quantum physics is the science of the very smallest things, like electrons.
An electron is a tiny particle that moves around the centre of an atom.
A laser makes a narrow beam of light, and short laser pulses can work like a super-fast camera.
Article_Structure: WHO: An international team of scientists in Regensburg and Hamburg.
WHAT: Scientists measured a new 'space-time limit' for electrons.
WHERE: In a lab in Germany, using a new laser system.
WHY: To watch electrons move and learn the speed limits of future electronics.
